items.stimulus: A seismologist models the positions of two monitoring stations and an earthquake epicenter as right triangle $PQR$. On a larger regional map, the same layout appears as triangle $STU$, and each side of triangle $STU$ is 3 times as long as the corresponding side of triangle $PQR$.
items.stem: Triangle $PQR$ is similar to triangle $STU$, where $P$, $Q$, and $R$ correspond to $S$, $T$, and $U$, respectively. Angle $R$ is a right angle, and $\sin P = \frac{5}{13}$. What is the value of $\sin S$?
items.explanation: Since $P$ corresponds to $S$, angles $P$ and $S$ are congruent. Congruent angles have the same sine, whatever the size of the triangle, so $\sin S = \sin P = \frac{5}{13}$.

A.why: You used the other acute angle. $\frac{12}{13}$ is $\cos P$, which equals $\sin Q$, so it would be $\sin T$. It is not $\sin S$, because $S$ corresponds to $P$.

C.why: You found $\tan P$, which is opposite over adjacent, $\frac{5}{12}$. The question asks for the sine.

D.why: You multiplied the sine by the scale factor of 3. A trig ratio compares two sides that both grow by the same factor, so it does not change between similar triangles. A sine can also never be greater than 1.
